title: The Five Questions Our Students Are Asking, All the Time
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Dave Stuart Jr. argues that student motivation is not fixed on Day One or Day 100 but ebbs and flows with students' answers to five largely unconscious questions. Each question maps to one of his key beliefs: Credibility (do I have a good teacher), Value (does this work matter), Effort (will my effort pay off), Efficacy (can I succeed), and Belonging (do people like me belong here). For each, he lists the sub-questions kids silently ask and links to a practical exercise, such as a pop-up debate for Value and a small-wins memorization task for Effort. He notes that teacher credibility carries one of the highest effect sizes in Hattie's work and that beliefs, not laziness, drive behavior. The piece is a compact diagnostic lens for teachers who want to read why a student is disengaged, though it closes with a promotion for his PD course.
points: Student motivation is a moving target shaped by five recurring, mostly unconscious questions, so teachers must keep answering them all year rather than only in the first week.
Each question corresponds to a named belief (Credibility, Value, Effort, Efficacy, Belonging), giving teachers a vocabulary for diagnosing why a particular student is checked out.
Value cannot be built with an occasional speech on why history or math matters; kids continually evaluate whether the work is worth their time against competing pulls like their phones.
Efficacy is complicated because students define success differently, from passing with a D- to needing a 93%, so teachers must help kids define success.
Belonging can be shifted by something as small as a shared birthday or a moment of genuine connection with the teacher.
quotes: All of our students, throughout the school year and especially at the start, are asking five questions. The level of motivation they'll bring to their work in our rooms isn't set in stone on Day One, or on Day 100.
Teacher credibility has one of the highest effect sizes in John Hattie's Visible Learning meta-analysis. Here are some ways to build it, and here are some ways to undermine it.
Teaching is a cool job because we get to experiment with Value cultivation every day. And our kids are required by law to come to our class and be our guinea pigs.

Hard work is hard, so us human beings typically need to believe it's going to pay off if we're going to do it in the first place. If I just believe that, no matter what, I'll never do 100 push-ups, then guess what? I probably won't do a single push-up today.

I've been talking with some of my students lately who are certain of the fact that they're going to transfer to the alternative high school as soon as they rack up enough failed classes. When I ask them why they're so bent on this, they say, “I can't learn in this high school.” This is the Efficacy belief's opposite: I'm sure that I will fail.
Students' sense of their belonging in our classes and schools can be affected by anything from sharing a birthday with someone else to experiencing moments of genuine connection with you.
